1. Revision History

XXX 2025 Published

2. Overview and Scope

This pairing project is a pilot effort to identify how a subset of EPA’s indicators of observed climate change align with historical and projected model data under a variety of plausible climate change scenarios. Projections come from the best available global climate models (GCMs), which, at the time of publication, were drawn from the World Climate Research Programme (WCRP) Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) suite. Steps have been taken to align projections with the corresponding observed indicator with respect to spatial coverage, spatial and temporal aggregation, and other indicator derivation steps (i.e., how physical measurements are transformed into an indicator). In simple terms, a successful alignment should allow projections and observations to be graphed or mapped in a common format. For example, an indicator represented by a time series in a line graph should be able to display projections as dashed lines continuing out into the future.

This effort focuses on variables that can be derived directly from GCM projections. Thus, it covers physical attributes of weather and climate, the oceans, and some aspects of the cryosphere. It does not include human or ecological impacts, nor does it include physical variables that would require supplementary modeling of dynamic responses or highly location-specific factors (for example, the response of ice sheets and small glaciers to continued warming). EPA’s separate Climate Change Impacts and Risk Analysis (CIRA) effort provides peer reviewed modeling of ecological, human health, societal, and economic impacts of future climate change.

The results from this effort are intended to complement EPA’s suite of observed climate change indicators. EPA’s observed indicators are the primary source of historical data. Other observation sources have been introduced in limited instances, where doing so was necessary to create a proper temporal, spatial, and definitional alignment with GCM projections.

Projection sources and methods were selected to align with the U.S. Global Change Research Program’s (USGCRP’s) Fifth National Climate Assessment, as described in more detail below.

3. Project Development

Feasibility Assessment

The project began with a feasibility assessment to identify the extent to which each of EPA’s observed metrics could be projected credibly into the future using the best available GCMs. Use of the term “metrics” here is intentional, as many of EPA’s indicators contain multiple metrics, sometimes reflecting a variety of sources, methods, units, and spatial and temporal characteristics. It is highly possible that a single EPA climate change indicator could include some metrics that are easily projectable and others that are not. To account for this, subsequent review examined each individual metric on its own merits. Altogether, the project team reviewed 143 metrics. For each metric, the assessment considered factors such as, but not limited to:

  • How the observed variable has been calculated or derived.
  • Whether the same variable can be calculated directly from GCM outputs. For example, EPA’s Ocean Acidity indicator includes a pH component that has been modeled by GCMs and an aragonite saturation component that has not.
  • The extent to which the projections will likely align with the observations. If the alignment is not perfect (for example, if it uses a different unit of measure, baseline, or calculation method), either the observed data set or the projections might require some degree of transformation to ensure compatibility. However, some cases might involve a less easily surmountable difference. For example, the project team anticipated a mismatch between observed and projected approaches for snowpack. Observations are point-based, projections are gridded, and the GCM grid is unlikely to capture the elevation, terrain, and microclimate effects that influence snowpack accumulation at any given long-term measurement site.
  • The number of CMIP6 GCMs with available data. Indicators with fewer than seven models available were excluded from further analysis.
  • Value added. For example, devoting the available resources to modeling a variety of topics was determined to be more useful than, say, modeling three different definitions of drought, focusing largely on greenhouse gas inputs, or focusing on one metric that requires a disproportionate share of resources to compute.

The project team used the results of this feasibility review to sort metrics into six bins, as shown in Table 1. The project team also identified at least 12 cases where an identical metric could not be calculated from GCM projections, but a similar metric could.

Table 1. Categories Assigned in Project Team’s Projection Feasibility Analysis

Category

Examples

Group 1: Calculate directly from a CMIP GCM input or output variable with no modifications

Group 2: Calculate from CMIP downscaled temperature and/or precipitation

Group 3: Projections available from a secondary model driven by GCM or downscaled CMIP projections

Ultimately, a subset of the metrics from Groups 1, 2, and 5 were selected for further analysis and publication. Additional variables may be integrated in the future.

Data Acquisition, Processing, and Review

The project team inspected and obtained data, calculated and aggregated projections to align with observed indicators, and checked each provisional alignment carefully. These steps are described in more detail below. If modeled results did not align well with historical observations, steps were taken to improve the alignment. If no credible steps could be taken to rectify a lack of alignment (i.e., to “close the gap”), the indicator was excluded from further consideration.

Peer Review

Methods and results underwent an independent peer review that followed the procedures in EPA’s Peer Review Handbook, 4th Edition (EPA/100/B-15/001) (U.S. EPA, 2015) for reports that do not provide influential scientific information. The review was managed by a contractor under the direction of a designated EPA peer review leader, who prepared a peer review plan, the scope of work for the review contract, and the charge for the reviewers. The peer review leader played no role in producing this product.

The peer review consisted of an external individual letter review by two climate science who had familiarity with USGCRP reports, general circulation models, observational datasets, downscaling approaches, applied statistics, and/or model evaluation. The two experts independently selected by an external contractor (ICF International) were Drs. Adrienne Wootten (University of Oklahoma) and Vaishali Naik (NOAA). These experts had no conflicts of interest.

The peer review charge asked reviewers to provide detailed comments and to assess if the project effectively communicated the purpose, methodology, and limitations of comparing observed indicators with climate model data. Reviewers requested a more detailed discussion of uncertainty, particularly regarding downscaling methods and inherent model limitations. This feedback was addressed by adding a dedicated section on downscaling uncertainty and incorporating language about model uncertainty into relevant indicators. Another concern raised was the inconsistency in baselines, time periods, and mapping divisions used across indicators. However, these differences reflect the structure of EPA’s existing observed indicator products, which represent the best available data from disparate sources. As this project’s goal was to align with those existing indicators, no changes were made in this area. The products were revised to address peer reviewers’ comments and a spreadsheet was prepared to document how each of the approximately 50 comments from the peer review was addressed.

4. Data Sources for Historical Observations

Historical observations primarily come from EPA’s existing suite of climate change indicators. Each indicator has a description of data sources and a corresponding technical documentation file that provides more specific details regarding direct source data, underlying data, metadata, data collection and processing methods, and how users can access data files. All of EPA’s indicators were screened and peer reviewed to ensure they fulfill a set of 10 data quality criteria. Key criteria include (but are not limited to) a requirement that the historical indicator data be based on actual measurements and provide long-term coverage that is comparable over time and space and suitable for analyzing trends.

The project team used existing EPA indicator data for these observation/projection pairings wherever possible. A few pairings used other historical sources due to methodological or definitional limitations or mismatches between the available projections and EPA’s existing indicators. Alternative data sources considered for this effort included NOAA’s nClimGrid Daily (1951–present for the contiguous United States) and nClimGrid Monthly (1895–present for the contiguous United States and Alaska). The nClimGrid products offer data on a 5-kilometer grid. Whenever an alternative observation source was used, the existing indicator’s methodological approach was replicated to the extent possible. Each observed/projected pairing’s detailed technical documentation file identifies specific historical data sources and the rationale for their selection.

5. Data Sources for Modeled Data

Model data for this effort come from the CMIP6 suite of GCMs. Four types of CMIP6-derived products were used, depending on what was most appropriate for each metric:

  • Group A: Direct outputs from the CMIP6 suite. This approach was used for metrics that can be readily calculated from GCM gridded outputs without a need for further downscaling, such as sea ice extent and snow cover. All raw CMIP6 GCM outputs used for this project were obtained from the publicly available CMIP6 data archive hosted by the Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF). The CMIP6 suite includes several dozen models or variations thereof; however, for consistency across metrics and consistency with other federal government efforts, this project used the same subset of 16 GCMs that were used for projections throughout the Fifth National Climate Assessment. Table 2 lists the 16 selected models and their sources. These 16 models were selected for the Fifth National Climate Assessment because they are the same 16 models for which STAR-ESDM and LOCA2 have downscaled projections. Spatial resolution of gridded outputs depends on various factors, but the GCMs overall use 0.5- to 1-degree pixels. The reason for using a suite of climate models is to capture model uncertainty and differences in climate sensitivity and variability between the models (Hawkins & Sutton, 2009). Individual GCMs perform multiple ensemble runs. For feasibility purposes, one ensemble run was used from each GCM—generally the first run that had the required variables. In most cases, this was the “r1i1p1f1” run.

  • Group B: Downscaled CMIP6 data. Several variables—namely, those that relate to air temperature and precipitation—can be downscaled to a higher-resolution grid for more robust and locally useful projections. Downscaled data were obtained from the Seasonal Trends and Analysis of Residuals Empirical-Statistical Downscaling Model (STAR-ESDM) (Hayhoe et al., 2024). STAR-ESDM is one of two downscaling approaches incorporated in the Fifth National Climate Assessment, with the other being Locally Constructed Analogs version 2 (LOCA2). Both are statistically downscaled ensemble products that provide a nominally 5-kilometer grid over the contiguous United States. Both have been trained using observed gridded products; STAR-ESDM using NOAA’s nClimGrid Daily and LOCA2 using the “Livneh” data sets from the University of Colorado’s Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences. Both STAR-ESDM and LOCA2 have been peer reviewed and validated (e.g., Ullrich et al., 2023). STAR-ESDM was selected for this project because its results were more readily accessible to the project team at the time of project development and reduced the cost associated with working with multiple data sets.

    STAR-ESDM has proven to be robust out to the 99th percentile of the distribution for both temperature and precipitation variables (Hayhoe et al., 2024). Independent evaluation of the downscaling approach and comparison with LOCA2 shows that the two methods, both state-of-the-art downscaled products, are largely in agreement with each other with some differences in the very extreme tails and in regions with large uncertainties in the observational data used, such as in mountain ranges (Ullrich, 2023; Hartke et al., 2025). Both methods display some dampening of future intensification of frontal precipitation events (Baek et al., 2024); however, that is not a focus of this effort and therefore not a cause for concern in this analysis.

    The STAR-ESDM effort has downscaled more than 20 GCMs. This effort used downscaled data from the same subset of 16 GCMs listed in Table 2 above. STAR-ESDM data are available for public download from: [link pending].

    The choice of downscaling approach introduces a source of uncertainty relating to the technique and data used in the downscaling model, which tends to be higher in areas with high topographical variation and for indicators describing climate extremes (e.g., Lafferty and Sriver, 2023; Wooten et al., 2017). There are many different dynamical and statistical downscaling models available, each with their respective level of uncertainty stemming from the observational data used to train the model as well as how well the downscaling model handles conditions in the climate that have never been observed, or changes in the relationship between the large-scale climate processes and local-scale responses to changes in those processes (i.e., climate stationarity). The proportion of uncertainty from the choice of downscaling approach is typically much smaller than the uncertainty due to spread among climate models and between different scenarios.

  • Group C: Updated sea level projections from NOAA. For sea level and coastal flooding, the federal government’s authoritative projections are those published and periodically updated by NOAA. This effort used the most recent NOAA projections available at the time of publication, which were published in NOAA’s 2022 report, Global and Regional Sea Level Rise Scenarios for the United States (Sweet et al., 2022).

    The NOAA team’s approach combines CMIP6 GCM outputs; multiple methods of projecting future changes in the ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland; projections for glaciers, land water storage, and other factors; and an understanding of vertical land motion to project future sea level and coastal flooding relative to the shoreline at specific locations along U.S. coasts. These same methods were used for the sea level projections in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Sixth Assessment Report (AR6), published in 2021 and 2022. NOAA’s report describes sources and methods in detail. The report, along with projection data and metadata, can be viewed and downloaded publicly at NOAA's website.

  • Group D: Inputs to the CMIP6 ensemble runs. Projections of greenhouse gas concentrations come from the official Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios that fed into the CMIP6 GCM runs described above. These projections can be downloaded publicly from the SSP Database (version 2.0, December 2018). See section 6, “Future Climate Scenarios,” for more details about the SSP scenarios.

6. Future Climate Scenarios

For metrics in Groups A, B, and D, projections for four distinct climate change scenarios are displayed to illustrate the range of possible future outcomes and to demonstrate why it is important that climate change solutions consider both mitigation and adaptation. Divergence of projected impacts over time show that actions to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions and reduce warming will make a noticeable difference, yet even the lowest-emissions scenarios have impacts that demonstrate a need for adaptation. Group C metrics also show multiple scenarios for the same reason, but they reflect a different set of scenarios because of the additional factors that NOAA’s team integrated into their modeling.

The Group A, B, and D data visualizations feature the four SSPs described in Table 3. These four SSPs were selected to provide a range of possible outcomes (as described above) in a manner consistent with the authoritative national and global assessments of climate change, as the climate science community has largely standardized on the use of these SSPs. The SSPs are defined by a set of socioeconomic development narratives and delineate future greenhouse gas emissions trajectories (Lamie et al., 2024 and O’Neill et al., 2014). The IPCC has not assigned likelihoods to these scenarios. The graphs and maps provide all four SSPs at face value. For effective communication, the SSPs in the observation/projection alignment product are referred to using consistent plain language names from the IPCC AR6 Summary for Policymakers, as listed in Table 3, rather than by their formal SSP numbers.

NOAA’s projections of sea level rise and coastal flooding use a different set of five scenarios, shown in Table 4. These scenarios do not correspond directly to the SSPs. However, Table 2.4 in NOAA’s technical report (Sweet et al., 2022) provides a comparison that includes each sea level scenario’s estimated probability of occurrence under different degrees of global mean surface air temperature change, which in turn are related back to the SSPs. NOAA’s “intermediate-low” and “intermediate” scenarios provide reasonable estimates of the lower and upper bounds for the most likely sea level rise by 2100, respectively. Thus, this effort focuses on these two scenarios. They have been labeled as “lower sea level rise” and “higher sea level rise” in the figures, to avoid confusion or conflation with the emissions scenarios shown in other figures. NOAA’s “intermediate-high” and “high” scenarios rely to a larger extent on low-confidence ice sheet processes in addition to high or very high greenhouse gas emissions.

In addition to projections of greenhouse gas concentrations, the SSP scenarios also include emissions projections for other gas and aerosol pollutants, such as sulfur dioxide and black carbon (IPCC, 2021). The presence of sulfur dioxide, a precursor for sulfate aerosols, has a cooling effect due to short-wave radiation from the sun being reflected back into space by the aerosol particles, whereas black carbon in the atmosphere can have a warming effect due to absorbing radiation. The net effect of anthropogenic aerosol emissions has been to cool the atmosphere. Thus, anthropogenic aerosol emissions have in some areas been able to mask or offset a portion of the warming caused by increases in greenhouse concentrations. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Chapter 1 (IPCC, 2021) shows projected decreases in anthropogenic emissions of aerosols over the next several decades, which as very likely to reduce their cooling offset and unmask greenhouse gas warming.

7. Temporal Considerations

This section describes a variety of considerations related to timeframes and temporal averaging.

Historical observations. Timeframes for historical observations are consistent with EPA’s climate change indicator suite. Decisions on how far back in time to display historical data reflect a thorough review of data availability, consistency, and comparability, and have been documented in each indicator’s peer reviewed technical documentation.

Projection horizon. NOAA’s 2022 projections for sea level and coastal flooding extend through 2150, so they are being shown over their full range. All other projections in this effort extend through 2100. This endpoint was selected because many GCM runs stop at 2100, so this time period offers the greatest richness of models to aggregate together. Projections for each indicator start from the end of the available observed indicator data. For example, if an indicator had observed data from 1950 to 2024, the climate projections would stretch from 2024 to 2100.

Scenario divergence and hindcasts. The SSPs and CMIP6 model runs used as a basis for this effort start to show divergence between scenarios in 2015. Modeled values prior to 2015 represent hindcasts and are shown as a single line on each graph. This part of the modeled data is referred to as a “hindcast” because it is run using observed greenhouse gas concentrations, volcanic forcing events, solar radiation variations, and aerosols. However, these hindcasts still include internal variability, such as El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events that will not align with the timing of ENSO events that were experienced in reality. The graphs show hindcasts back to 1950 as well as any prior years for which both the observed indicator and the hindcast had data available for comparison. In general, downscaled STAR variables had hindcasts available back to 1950, while non-downscaled GCM outputs could go back as far as 1850. Comparing actual observations with concurrent hindcasts can illustrate how accurately the models represent the climate phenomena in question, it gives a sense of how well scientists understand the historical changes in those indicators, and it is a vital step in aligning historical observations and future projections for this effort. Meanwhile, comparing historical observations with the modeled projections allows the audience to calibrate their lived experiences of historical change against the magnitude of changes seen in future climate model output.

Averaging. In climate modeling, it is common to report and visualize projections that are averaged over 10- to 30-year windows, in part to capture year-to-year variability and to avoid implying false year-to-year precision in the models. The decision to average projections is largely a question of how one presents and visualizes results, as the models themselves provide outputs at annual or sub-annual resolution. For this effort, unless noted otherwise, projections are generally displayed as 11-year moving averages in line graphs (i.e., a data point is plotted at each year, reflecting an arithmetic mean of the 11 years centered that point in time). Endpoints are not padded, so the last 11-year average (2090–2100) is plotted at 2095, and the line graphs plot no data for 2096–2100. Similar smoothing is applied to the blended model hindcast, which means the last hindcast value is plotted at 2009, as 2014 was the last year before scenarios began to diverge. This smoothing, along with multi-model averaging, is why the model data displayed in these graphs typically look smoother than the historical trends.

Baselines. Some of EPA’s observed indicators report anomalies relative to a specific historical baseline period. For alignment, projections should be presented in reference to the same baseline. If such alignment was not possible in certain cases (for example, if modeled data were not available for the entire period needed to establish the baseline), projections were shifted based on a shared period of overlap (see the “delta method” in section 8 below) or both observed and projected data were shifted to a new common baseline. The technical documentation for each observation/projection pairing describes any such shifts in detail.

For maps, total change was calculated from the end of the observed data record through 2100. For example, if an indicator has observed data through 2020, the map would calculate total projected change from 2021 to 2100.

8. Calculation, Alignment, and Data Transformation Methods

Each indicator/model data pairing page provides access to a technical document that discusses specific methods in detail. Therefore, this section of the general technical documentation focuses instead on general calculation steps and approaches shared across the entire project. The descriptions below cover an overarching sequence of steps.

  1. Calculate the intended metric for each model. The project team attempted to apply the same definition and calculation methods that were used in the corresponding observed indicator. For example, the Seasonal Temperature indicator used daily mean temperatures averaged over each meteorological season, while developing the Marine Heat Waves pairing involved running GCM outputs through the same script that EPA’s observed indicator uses to first establish location-specific, percentile-based thresholds, and then identify four-consecutive-day events that exceeded these thresholds.

    The gridded projections were analyzed to match the spatial coverage and resolution of the observed indicator. With respect to coverage, the team used geographic information systems (GIS) software to clip the projections to the target domain and to mask land or non-land grid cells or portions thereof, where needed. With respect to resolution, at one extreme, certain metrics required all grid cells to be averaged over a large area, such as the contiguous United States. In such cases, the necessary averaging was done in GIS software, using appropriate area weighting to account for partial grid cells and for latitudinal effects on cell size. At the other extreme, metrics such as pH required data to be selected from a specific subset of modeled grid cells that correspond to the point locations where historical measurements have been collected.

  1. Adjust baselines for comparability, if needed. Many of EPA’s observed indicators use a defined historical baseline period as a basis for reporting anomalies or change. Others use a historical baseline period to derive thresholds for comparison, such as those necessary to define location-specific “average” conditions for a drought index and those necessary to define what constitutes an “extreme” event. Aligning future projections with these historical observations requires that the projections refer to the same baseline. Where possible, the project team calculated the projected metric with respect to the modeled hindcast values for the same baseline period.

    The project team encountered some situations where the observed indicator’s defined baseline period extended outside the temporal range of modeled data. That is, the modeled hindcasts did not extend back far enough in time to cover the full baseline period that must be used to compute the indicator. The solution depended on the nature of each case, as the following examples illustrate:

    • EPA’s Length of Growing Season indicator reports anomalies relative to the average over the entire observed data set (1895–present), whereas hindcasts for the full set of GCMs are available back to only 1951. Because this indicator only uses a baseline to report anomalies, and because the variable in question represents an absolute measure (number of days), it is straightforward and defensible to simply pick a new common baseline period and reset the indicator to it. This essentially means shifting one or both series up or down on the graph, adding or subtracting a constant across all years. It does not change the shape of the curve or the slope of any resulting trends. In practice, projections could be shifted this way while leaving the historical observation data consistent with the way they are presented in EPA’s published indicators.
    • EPA’s U.S. and Global Precipitation indicator calculates precipitation anomalies and percent change relative to a 1901–2000 baseline period, whereas hindcasts for the full set of GCMs are again available back to only 1951. Percent change does not allow curves to be simply shifted up or down on the graph by a constant as described in the previous example. Thus, percent change was recalculated for the historical observations relative to a 1951–2000 baseline, then applied the same baseline period with the GCM outputs. This affects the map of percent change, but not the time-series graph that uses anomalies in inches.
    • Figure 1 of EPA’s Heavy Precipitation indicator comes from NOAA’s Climate Extremes Index (CEI), which defines extreme events relative to percentile thresholds derived from the entire period of record, which begins in 1910. With hindcasts available back to 1951, and without the flexibility to redefine the CEI to use a different baseline period, no further analysis or alignment was pursued for this indicator. Use of a different observed data source in the future could reopen the potential for alignment with GCM projections.

    In general, where a new baseline period was needed for recalculations, a 1951–2000 baseline was used.

  1. Calculate a multi-model mean. Projections for Group A and B variables came from up to 16 GCMs. Authoritative assessments have traditionally weighted GCMs in a prescribed way when calculating central estimates. For this effort, the same weighting approach used in the Fifth National Climate Assessment was used: a Bayesian weighting approach documented by Massoud et al. (2023). This approach calculates a weight for each model based on factors that include the individual models’ equilibrium and transient climate response consistent with assessed estimates of Earth’s climate sensitivity (Massoud et al., 2023). Note that this approach does not eliminate outlier models (if any) from being included in the average, but models that deviate further from what is deemed a realistic or expected sensitivity are given lower weights compared with models that have a climate sensitivity closer to the expected value. The weights given to each model depend on the specific set of models in the ensemble, such that their combined weight sums to 1.

    For variables that only had projections from a subset of the 16 GCMs, the authors of Massoud et al. (2023) were consulted. They provided a custom Bayesian weighting for the subset, following the same principles as the 16-GCM weighting approach.

    Group C variables reflect a multi-GCM blending that was conducted by NOAA’s project team and published in NOAA’s 2022 technical report prior to inclusion in this effort.

    Group D, projected greenhouse gas concentrations, represents a common set of inputs to all the models. Thus, no multi-model aggregation was needed.

  1. Calculate a range of modeled values. For Group A and B metrics, the line graphs included a shaded band around each SSP to offer users a sense of the range of projections available from different GCMs. This range includes the 10th to 90th percentiles of the distribution of results from individual models (up to 16 models). This approach is widely used to show the spread of plausible outcomes and acknowledge the uncertainty inherent in future projections (a key reason for incorporating more than a dozen different models) while omitting any true outliers. These ranges were calculated based on annual projected values, without applying any multi-year smoothing.

    For Group C topics (sea level and coastal flooding), figures with ranges show the 17th to 83rd percentiles as reported by NOAA.

    Group D (projected greenhouse gas concentrations) is inherently a single set of inputs shared across all GCMs, so there is no range of values to show around each SSP. Here, the spread among the four SSPs constitutes the most relevant range to show.

  1. Check alignment. Projections and historical observations were plotted in the same format and their degree of alignment over the time period in which the observations overlap with modeled hindcasts or (for the most recent years) SSP projections was considered. The extent to which the time series appears to transition from observed to projected, or whether the transition shows continuity or a notable “step” that suggests a discontinuity, has been documented. This step primarily involved visual comparison, though the project team also used some simple quantitative comparisons (e.g., percent difference) to characterize the degree of alignment or deviation. As somewhat of a pilot exercise, this effort did not use more involved statistical techniques to test alignment.
  1. Transform as needed. The project team took steps to achieve credible pairings between historical observations and projections. Specific steps are described in each pairing’s technical documentation, but they generally followed the hierarchy below:

    2. Good alignment: If the previous step revealed projections reasonably well aligned with the historical observations, the results were plotted and published with no further transformation. Figure TD-1 shows an example for sea surface temperature. After converting units and calculating anomalies with respect to the same 30-year baseline, the authors found that observed and modeled results aligned reasonably well.

    Figure TD-1. Global mean sea surface temperature alignment example

    Moderate lack of alignment: The project team investigated further to determine if the apparent discontinuity between observations and projections could be a symptom of a mismatch in how the data were processed or calculated. Figure TD-2 shows an example of a mismatch for snow cover. This figure depicts the annual average snow-covered area over all of North America excluding Greenland; the authors found similar mismatches for individual seasons. In this case, further investigation included discussion with the Rutgers Global Snow Lab, which had provided the observed data analysis to the project team. The original Rutgers product was derived from satellite imagery using a relatively coarse grid for analysis, but Rutgers provided a prototype product they had developed using a higher-resolution grid, and it aligned much more closely with GCM outputs, closing the gap by approximately half in all seasons. The project team proceeded with the higher-resolution observations for this pairing and made plans to update the Snow Cover indicator on EPA’s website with the new source once Rutgers officially publishes it. This still left a gap between observed and modeled time series, possibly related to different calculation methods required for the larger grid cells in the model outputs, so a straightforward vertical shift was applied—a bias correction using the well-established “delta method.” All GCM outputs (hindcast and future projections) were shifted up by a constant amount to align the observed and modeled 1979–2014 means.

    In other cases, an apparent mismatch did not have such an obvious explanation related to definitions or methods. It could well be that the GCMs simply do not represent a particular process or attribute as accurately as they represent a more fundamental measure like surface temperature, or that different cell sizes between the observed and modeled grids skewed the analysis. Monthly average Arctic sea ice extent is one such example. Extent is defined as the total areal coverage of pixels that are at least 15 percent frozen. After confirming that the models were using the same definition as the observed indicator, the authors noted that there was still a persistent gap between observations and modeled outputs (Figure TD-3), but, importantly, the two curves follow a nearly identical shape. This diagnosis made Arctic sea ice a candidate for a bias correction. In this case, a multiplicative shift was applied, adjusting all GCM outputs (hindcast and future projections) up by a constant ratio to align the observed and modeled 1979–2014 means. In this case, a multiplicative bias correction was more effective than an additive correction at retaining the accuracy of an eventual asymptote—where sea ice extent reaches a near-zero level in the warmest scenarios. Figure TD-3 shows the result of this transformation.

    Figure TD-2. Snow cover alignment example

    Figure TD-3. Arctic sea ice alignment example

    Poor alignment: If observed and modeled results were highly out of alignment, and/or the curves were of a notably different shape, and no reasonable solution could be found (e.g., a different source, better alignment of methods, or bias correction), the project team did not proceed with the pairing.

9. Communication

For each indicator/projection pairing, the project team has created a webpage that presents the following content:

  • One or more graphs or maps that allow the audience to view historical observations and associated future projections in a common frame. These figures are interactive. On graphs, interactivity allows the audience to toggle specific series on or off, drill down into specific scenarios where possible, and hover to display numbers. On maps, interactivity allows the audience to pan, zoom in and out, and select data points on vector-format maps (points, polygons). Specific graphics have been designed to display a compelling but not overwhelming amount of information by default and to use terms, labels, and visualization practices that make the information accessible to a wide audience. For example, this project intentionally uses English/imperial units in many cases, rather than metric. Colors for the four SSP scenarios have been standardized across figures and aligned with the colors used in the IPCC AR6 Summary for Policymakers. Where shaded bands are used, they depict the range between the 10th and 90th percentiles of all the individual models that were run.
  • Background text. Contextual information about the topic is intentionally brief, as readers can find deeper discussion within each of the indicators on EPA's climate change indicators website.
  • Key points that briefly summarize the shape of the data, notable patterns or trends, maxima and minima, differences between scenarios, and other attributes that can help readers interpret the “story” that the data are telling. The text generally describes the direction and magnitude of change but does not present detailed trend analysis, as that was outside the scope of this pilot exercise. This section can also introduce additional insights from the scientific literature that provide useful context for understanding. Preference is given to authoritative IPCC and USGCRP assessments, where possible.
  • Sources and methods. Each indicator page summarizes this information for quick reference but points readers to a technical documentation file if they seek more details.
